title: Strength Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: Strength upright: courage, patience, gentleness; reversed: self-doubt or calm worn thin. Love, work, advice, Waite's 1911 text and the 1909 card. Draw it.
image_alt: Strength, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a woman in white with flowers in her hair holds the jaws of an orange-red lion, a figure-eight loop above her head and a blue mountain behind.
capsule: Strength is card VIII of the Major Arcana: courage, patience and a gentleness that holds steady. Reversed, it points to self-doubt or calm worn thin. A kind, encouraging card, it values soft power over force and asks for kindness toward yourself. The lion is calmed without a fight, and that is why the card answers yes when upright.

blocks.heading: What is on the Strength card?
paragraphs: A woman in a white dress bends over a lion and holds its jaws with both hands. Waite describes her as "closing the jaws of a lion" and says the design departs from older ones in a single point: "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers" (p. 100).

The lion is the biggest thing in the picture: orange-red, with a mane of tight curls, it fills most of the lower half on the 1909 card. The woman wears flowers in her hair, and a garland of them winds around her waist and down toward the lion.

Above her head floats a loop shaped like a figure eight; for Waite it is a "symbol of life" (p. 100). Behind the pair the background is plain yellow, a small blue mountain rises in the distance, and the numeral VIII sits at the top.

Waite notes that older cards usually showed the figure "closing the mouth of a lion", while in one earlier form "she is obviously opening it"; either way, he says, the image "conveys the idea of mastery" (p. 16).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about Strength?
paragraphs: Waite's upright list is bright from start to finish: power, energy, courage, generosity of spirit ("magnanimity"), even success and honours. The reversed list shows that power going wrong, used to dominate rather than to hold, or giving way to weakness and discord.

He warned against reading the card too simply. It "has nothing to do with self-confidence in the ordinary sense", he wrote; it concerns "the confidence of those whose strength is God" (p. 103). He also linked it to "the strength which resides in contemplation" (p. 100). In one aspect, he adds, "the lion signifies the passions" (p. 103).

blocks.heading: What does Strength mean upright?
paragraphs: Upright, Strength speaks of courage that does not need to shout. It is patience with something difficult, steady nerves, the choice to stay kind while you hold your ground. The card tends to come up when a situation, or a feeling inside you, seems wild and the first urge is to fight it.

The picture offers another way. The woman does not wrestle the lion; she closes its jaws with bare hands and a calm face. Gentleness here is not weakness but the thing that lets strength last. Meet what feels unruly with kindness and persistence rather than pressure.
This inner strength works on you as much as on anything outside. A question worth trying: what in me needs a firm hand, and what needs a soft one?

blocks.heading: What does Strength mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, Strength can point to self-doubt: the courage is still there, but right now it does not feel like yours. Or a gentle nature may be worn thin from holding everything together, until old fears and frustration sound louder than usual.
In Waite's second list the trouble is power misused, or weakness. The tired, overstretched side is a modern reading, not Waite's.

Neither version calls for more effort. Be patient with yourself first, notice where you are losing patience with yourself or with others, and let courage come back through small acts rather than one big push.

blocks.heading: What does Strength mean in love?
paragraphs: Tenderness that does not erase you: that is the woman's hold on the lion, and it is how this card loves. Between partners, it favors gentle honesty: saying what you need calmly, setting limits with warmth, staying soft without giving yourself away.
Without a partner, the card suggests patience with your own heart: letting closeness grow at a pace that feels safe, without hiding who you are.
Drawn reversed, the card may show strain from keeping the peace too long, or self-doubt that makes you shrink. What would one calm, honest sentence about your needs sound like?

blocks.heading: What does Strength mean for work and money?
paragraphs: On the job, steady influence does more than pressure under this card: handling a tense moment calmly, staying patient with slow progress, leading by example. It suits places where force would backfire and persistence would not.
Before you spend or save, notice where your choices come from: calm, or a wish to get an uncomfortable feeling over with quickly?
Upside down, the card asks where self-doubt keeps you from speaking up, or where you push too hard on something that needs time.

blocks.heading: What is Strength's advice?
paragraphs: When something frustrates you, lower your voice and slow down instead of pushing harder. Answer pressure with calm: take one deep breath, then choose the gentlest firm step within reach.

blocks.heading: Is Strength a yes or no card?
Strength as a person and as a feeling
paragraphs: Think of the woman with the lion when this card stands for someone: a calm, kind person who quietly holds things steady when they get hard. About you, it shows your patient, brave side, the one that has nothing to prove. The feeling is warm steadiness; reversed, it is closer to tiredness, or nerves near fraying.

pairs.text: Will and gentleness together. Move forward firmly, but let patience set the pace.
Patience from two sides. Small, steady adjustments work better than any grand gesture.
Resilience on a long stretch. Rest where you can and keep a soft grip on the goal.
Courage facing self-doubt. The way out starts with one small brave act.

blocks.heading: Strength or The Chariot?
paragraphs: Both cards are about mastery. The Chariot shows a crowned figure whose chariot is pulled by two sphinxes, and Waite calls him "triumph in the mind" (p. 96); the modern meaning is will and direction. Strength shows a woman calming a lion by hand. The Chariot keeps opposing forces in line through focus; Strength wins the lion over with patience and gentleness. When you need to push ahead, The Chariot fits; when you need to soften a struggle, Strength does.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about Strength
paragraphs: Where am I using force when patience would work better?
What part of me needs gentleness instead of criticism?
What small brave thing could I do today?

faq.q: Is Strength a good or bad card?
faq.a: Good, and one of the kindest cards to draw. Courage, calm and the patience that wins over a hard situation instead of crushing it are all on its side. The risk it names is overdoing that softness, being kind to everyone except yourself. Reversed, it asks you to rest, not to try harder.

In this deck it is 8. Waite says the card "has been interchanged with that of Justice, which is usually numbered eight", for reasons he keeps to himself: the change, he says, carries nothing that will signify to the reader (p. 100). His lists elsewhere in the book also give Fortitude as 8 (pp. 16, 284). On Arcana Diary, Strength is card VIII and Justice card XI.

faq.q: Does Strength mean being physically strong?
faq.a: Rarely. In Part I Waite records that the figure has been said to stand for "organic force, moral force and the principle of all force" (p. 16). Here the card leans to the moral side: nerve, steadiness, the ability to stay calm with something wild.

faq.q: Does Strength mean I have to hold everything together?
faq.a: No. That burden belongs to the reversed side, where gentleness wears out from carrying too much. Upright, real strength includes asking for help and resting when you need to. Holding a lion's jaws calmly is not the same as holding up the whole world alone.

waite.quote: Power, energy, action, courage, magnanimity; also complete success and honours. Reversed: Despotism, abuse of power, weakness, discord, sometimes even disgrace.
